 No Voter Or Candidate Has Vested Right Of Reservation In A Particular Constituency; Govt's Discretion Over Rotation : Supreme Court
 Debby Jain 
 16 Nov 2026 12:43 PM IST
 Share this 
 Listen to this Article The Supreme Court today observed that no voter or candidate has a vested right to have a particular constituency reserved for Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe. Further, rotation of the reserved seats shall be as per discretion of the government. 
 A bench of Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana was dealing with a challenge to Rule 12 of the Maharashtra Zilla Parishads and Panchayat Samitis (Manner and Rotation of Reservation of Seats) Rules, 2025. The petitioner initially moved the Bombay High Court for striking down of the Rule as violative of Article 14 of the Constitution, however, vide the impugned order, the petition was dismissed. 
 The High Court observed that no person could claim any right of reservation to a particular seat. Further, there was a change in the percentage of population since the last census. 
 "In this regard, it is necessary to mention here that the State Government for the first time has decided to change the areas of constituencies and therefore, the new constituencies would definitely get changed on the basis of geographical limits. Consequently, reservation of seat would also be changed. Therefore, as on today, it cannot be said that whether particular area would be reserved for particular category or not. The guesswork which the petitioners have done is not the ground to declare Rule (XII) as contrary to the Constitution or arbitrary on its face." 
 During today's hearing, Senior Advocate Vipin Sanghi (for petitioner) argued that Rule 12 rendered the concept of rotation illusory. He highlighted that the petitioner belonged to a constituency which had never been reserved. Just when the constituency's turn to be reserved came, the respondents said that the process would be started afresh. 
 Responding to the submission, Justice Bagchi said: "Rule 4(2) of 1961 Rules and Article 243(r) speak of rotation but the mechanism of rotation is within the discretion of the state government and that is where Rule 12 is within the jurisdiction of the state government". 
 Sanghi then clarified that the petitioner was not going into the validity of the Rule. "They have played fraud. I am in a constituency where percentage is low. This has never been reserved. When my turn to be reserved comes, they say we will start afresh. Which means that this constituency would never get reservation" , the senior counsel stressed. 
 Justice Bagchi then remarked, "Do you have a right to have your constituency reserved? No. It is the cutoff date. It can always be shifted by the government" . "Can the state take away the rotation which has been going on?" Sanghi queried in response. 
 Ultimately, the bench dismissed the special leave petition, clarifying that the order shall not stand in the way of the petitioner's representation to reconsider the scheme of rotation. The order was dictated thus, 
 "We have considered the submission advanced by Mr Sanghi that Rule 12 of the 1961 Rules, having shifted the cutoff date for rotation of constituencies for the purpose of reservation, make the very concept of rotation illusory. Though the argument is attractive at the first blush, the same fails to take into consideration that no voter or candidate can have a vested right to have a particular constituency reserved. 
 What the Constitution and 1961 Rules prescribe is a proportionate reservation of seats vis-a-vis the proportion of SC/ST in the total population of the local body concerned. 
 It is nobody's case that the reservation of seats for SC/ST have followed the same proportion vis-a-vis population. It is also correct that [...] prescribes a rotation of the reserved seats as per descending order of the SC/ST population. However, the manner and the time frame within which such reservation and such rotation is to be made is only within the discretion of the government and in exercise of such discretion, Rule 12 prescribed the next prospective election post 2025 Amendment as the first election. 
 We find no reason to hold that said Rule runs counter to either the concept of reservation of rotation of seats. Dismissed. Needless to mention, dismissal of the petition shall not stand in the way of the petitioner's representation for reconsideration of the scheme of rotation of reserved seats as per law." 
 The petition was filed through AoR Anagha S Desai.
